title: Shared letters, gaps allowed
hook: ABCBDAB and BDCABA share only 2 letters side by side. Allow gaps: how many now?

knows: a grid of smaller answers can solve edit distance (flaw-to-lawn)
doesNotKnow: that "what do two strings share, in order" is a different grid with a different cell rule
that a shared sequence may have gaps, so it can be longer than any shared block

misconception: The longest shared stretch is a block of letters side by side in both strings.
objective: The learner can fill the longest-common-subsequence grid for ABCBDAB and BDCABA (match: diagonal + 1; mismatch: larger of up and left), read 4 at the corner, trace back BCBA, and explain why it beats the longest shared block (2).

claims.text: The longest block of letters side by side in both ABCBDAB and BDCABA is 2 letters (AB or BD).
claims.source: Builder's node check (2026-10-14): every start pair compared letter by letter; longest common substring length 2, exactly AB and BD. Demo.tsx BLOCK recomputes the length. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Own node (scratchpad fc21/lcs.mjs): every substring of ABCBDAB tested against BDCABA; longest shared block length 2, exactly AB and BD. Reveal prints BLOCK.length = 2.

claims.text: Keeping order but allowing gaps, the longest sequence picked from both strings has 4 letters, and no 5-letter sequence is shared.
claims.source: Builder's node check (2026-10-14): grid fill gives 4 at the corner; brute force over all 127 subsequences of ABCBDAB and 63 of BDCABA gives maximum common length 4, with exactly three answers BCAB, BCBA, BDAB. Matches the brief (cs.algorithms.md #47). Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Own brute force over all 127 and 63 non-empty subsequences: max common length 4, answers exactly BCAB, BCBA, BDAB; no 5-letter common subsequence. Grid corner L[7][6] = 4.

claims.text: Each cell asks whether its two letters match: if so, it is the diagonal + 1; if not, it is the larger of the cell above and the cell to the left.
claims.source: CLRS 4th ed. section 14.4 (longest common subsequence, recurrence for c[i, j]); 3rd ed. section 15.4. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Recurrence re-derived (optimal substructure: if the last letters match, an LCS ends with that letter; if not, it drops a last letter from one string) and matches Demo.tsx L fill and the per-cell note. CLRS not opened (no copy reachable); placement 3e 15.4 confirmed only via course-notes search snippet (Bowdoin CS231 'LCS (CLRS 15.4)'); 4e 14.4 from memory. The sentence does not depend on the book. | REVISED v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): step message now reads e.g. 'Best for A vs B. A ≠ B: larger of up (0) and left (0) = 0.'; reveal sentence now opens 'Your first steps showed it: each cell asked one small question'; rule text unchanged. Unverified.

claims.text: Each cell holds the length of the longest shared sequence of the first letters of each string, so the corner answers for the whole strings.
claims.source: CLRS 4th ed. section 14.4: c[i, j] is the LCS length of the prefixes X_i and Y_j. Stage wording: 'Each cell: the best answer for the first letters of each string.' Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Follows from the recurrence by induction on i + j: L[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i letters of ABCBDAB and first j of BDCABA, so L[7][6] answers for the whole strings. Stage text 'Each cell: the best answer for the first letters of each string' matches. CLRS not opened (see c3). | REVISED v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): stage now also labels each stepped cell with its prefixes, e.g. 'Best for ABC vs BD.' (first i letters of ABCBDAB vs first j letters of BDCABA). Unverified.

claims.text: Tracing back from the corner (diagonal on a match, otherwise to the larger neighbour, up on a tie) picks B, C, B, A: 4 letters in this order in both strings.
claims.source: Builder's node check (2026-10-14): traceback with ties going up visits matches at rows 2, 3, 4, 6 and columns 1, 3, 5, 6, spelling BCBA (same as CLRS PRINT-LCS tie rule). Demo.tsx PICKS recomputes it. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Own traceback with up-on-tie: matches at (row, col) (2,1) (3,3) (4,5) (6,6), spelling BCBA, 4 letters; BCBA is a subsequence of both (own check). Demo PICKS/WORD use the same rule; reveal prints 'B, C, B, A'.

claims.text: Diff tools that show what changed between two files are built on this idea.
claims.source: Hunt and McIlroy 1976, 'An algorithm for differential file comparison', Bell Labs CSTR 41 (Unix diff finds a longest common subsequence of lines); Myers 1986, 'An O(ND) difference algorithm and its variations', Algorithmica 1. 'Built on this idea' means LCS, not this exact grid fill. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. Hunt and McIlroy 1976, Bell Labs CSTR 41: web-search summary of the paper (hosted at cs.dartmouth.edu/~doug/diff.pdf, PDF itself not reachable here) says diff's central method is finding a longest common subsequence of lines. Myers 1986 not checked; not needed for 'built on this idea'.

claims.text: The grid has 42 cells to fill: 7 rows by 6 columns.
claims.source: ABCBDAB has 7 letters and BDCABA has 6; 7 x 6 = 42 inner cells, the extra row and column of zeros are given. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): VERIFIED. 7 letters x 6 letters = 42 inner cells; Demo CELLS = R * C = 42 and stage reads 'Cell n of 42'; row 0 and column 0 are pre-filled zeros.

recall.question: In the shared-letters grid, the two letters for a cell do not match. What goes in the cell?
options: The larger of the cell above and the cell to the left
Zero, since the run of matching letters is broken
recall.why: A mismatch means one of the two letters is dropped, so the cell keeps the better of dropping it from either string: the larger of up and left. Gaps are allowed, so nothing resets to zero.
